title: Dark Caracal
summary: Dark Caracal is the name given to a mobile focused espionage activity set described in public reporting from 2018, which assessed it as operating from a state security service in Lebanon while noting that this attribution is contested and carries only limited confirmation. The group is unusual because its collection targets handsets rather than desktop networks. Reported tradecraft includes trojanised copies of popular messaging and social applications distributed outside official application stores, lures delivered through social media and chat, and infrastructure hosted on common cloud services so that beacons blend into ordinary mobile traffic. The malware abused broad application permissions to read messages, contacts, call logs, location and camera or microphone data, then uploaded the results to attacker controlled servers. Reported targeting covered military, government, activist, journalist and legal communities across many countries, with much of the collection aimed at personal accounts that sit outside corporate controls. Evidence is found in mobile device management or enterprise mobility records rather than classic endpoint telemetry: unexpected sideloaded applications, excessive permission requests, unusual outbound connections from handsets, and message archives leaving the network in unexpected formats. Investigators should record device and account context early, because mobile evidence is easily destroyed by a simple factory reset. A common misunderstanding is that a mature security programme covers phones; in most organisations it does not, and personal accounts are where the sensitive conversations actually live.

beginner.definition: Dark Caracal is a name used for a spying group that targets mobile phones. Public reporting from 2018 linked it to a state security service in Lebanon, but experts disagree about that link. The group is known for handing out fake versions of popular chat and social apps. Those apps then read private messages and photos.
beginner.whyItMatters: Most security teams protect laptops and servers, not phones. A phone follows your staff everywhere and holds their private chats. If a fake app is installed, an attacker can read messages that never touch the company network. That means the leak can continue even when every office system is well protected.
howItWorks: The attacker builds a fake copy of a popular chat or social media application.
The fake app is offered through a website, a chat message or a direct download link.
The victim installs it, often because it looks like a useful or familiar product.
The app asks for wide permissions such as messages, contacts, location and camera.
It sends the collected data to a server that hides behind a normal cloud service.
Updates keep the fake app working and the attacker keeps long term access to the phone.
beginner.example: Think about a food delivery rider who arrives with a paper bag printed with your favourite restaurant logo. The bag is correct, the price is correct, and the food smells right. Only the restaurant never sent this order, and the rider now knows your address and your door code. A fake mobile application works the same way. The name and the icon are real. The official store never published this app, and its owner now receives everything you type.
takeaways: Install applications only from official stores, and check the publisher name carefully.
Look at app permissions and remove anything that asks for far more than it needs.
Treat phones and personal accounts as part of your security scope, not outside it.

objectives: Explain why mobile devices and personal accounts are valuable intelligence targets.
Describe how trojanised applications outside official stores reach victims.
Identify which application permissions create the greatest risk on a handset.
Describe the mobile specific evidence to preserve before a device is reset.
State that public attribution for this group is contested and limited in confidence.
